metadata.title: Seedance 2.5 Prompt Guide: Formula & Copyable Examples
metadata.description: Write better Seedance 2.5 prompts with a practical shot formula, timecoded examples, camera language, audio cues and troubleshooting steps.

hero.label: Prompt field manual
hero.title: Seedance 2.5 prompt guide: formula, timecodes and examples
hero.description: A good Seedance 2.5 prompt names six things in order: subject, action, setting, camera, look and audio. Use one subject, one main action and one camera move with an endpoint. Add time ranges such as [0-5s] only when the shot has separate beats.
hero.verdict: Clarity beats adjective density. Start with one subject, one primary action and one camera move; add constraints only to solve a visible problem.
hero.last_reviewed: Templates reviewed October 12, 2026 · samples generated October 3
hero.source_note: Examples are original editorial guidance, not guaranteed outputs. Model results remain probabilistic; use short tests before committing credits to long, high-resolution clips.

quick_facts.label: Core formula
quick_facts.description: Subject, action, setting, camera, look, audio.

quick_facts.label: Long clips
quick_facts.description: Assign one visible beat to each interval.

quick_facts.label: First test
quick_facts.description: Diagnose motion before extending the shot.

quick_facts.label: Avoid
quick_facts.description: Do not request several camera moves at once.

steps.title: Subject
steps.description: Name the person, object or environment that must remain visually stable.

steps.title: Action
steps.description: Use a concrete verb and describe what changes from the beginning to the end.

steps.title: Setting
steps.description: Define the location, time of day and environmental motion that matters.

steps.title: Camera
steps.description: Choose shot size, lens feeling and one primary move with a start and stop.

steps.title: Look
steps.description: Specify lighting, palette, texture and realism without piling on incompatible styles.

steps.title: Audio
steps.description: Describe ambience, effects or dialogue intent only when audio generation is enabled.

examples.label: Single-shot formula
examples.text: A bicycle courier in a cobalt rain jacket accelerates through a wet night market. Low tracking shot beside the rear wheel, 35mm documentary feel, warm stall light reflected on asphalt, realistic spray and fabric movement, distant vendors and tire hiss, no music.

sections.title: Seedance 2.5 prompt examples
paragraphs: Additional unedited examples explore dialogue, animation and a timecoded sequence. These are individual outputs, not a reliability benchmark.

sections.title: Use timecodes for visible beats
paragraphs: Time ranges help when a shot contains sequential actions. Each interval should describe something the viewer can see or hear. Do not use timecodes to repeat styling words.

examples.label: 15-second narrative beat
examples.text:
[0–4s] Wide shot: a lone botanist enters a foggy glasshouse carrying a dim lantern; camera slowly cranes down.
[4–10s] She brushes a giant leaf; blue bioluminescent veins wake and travel across the plant, reflected in her eyes.
[10–15s] Camera arcs behind her as the entire glasshouse pulses awake; humid ambience, leaf movement, one low resonant tone.

examples.label: 10-second product reveal
examples.text:
[0–3s] Locked macro of condensation on an unbranded amber bottle, hard rim light on black.
[3–7s] Slow half-orbit as the bottle rotates once; liquid catches a warm highlight.
[7–10s] Movement settles into a clean hero frame, subtle room tone, no text, no extra objects.

sections.title: Write camera direction that can be executed

rows: Reveal context
Start close, slowly dolly back to a wide shot
Asking for zoom, orbit and crane simultaneously
Follow action
Low lateral tracking shot, matched to the runner's pace
Saying only cinematic camera
Build attention
Slow push-in that stops at a medium close-up
No endpoint or subject named
Show an object
Controlled 120-degree clockwise orbit, stable product geometry
Requesting a full spin in too little time
Documentary energy
Handheld shoulder-height follow, small natural corrections
Combining handheld with perfectly locked framing

sections.title: Diagnose common failures before adding more words

rows: Subject changes identity
Too many subjects or weak reference priority
Reduce the cast; put identity first; use a clean reference
Camera move is ignored
Move conflicts with action or has no endpoint
Use one move and state where it stops
Shot feels static
Prompt describes appearance but no change
Add one physical action with a clear beginning and end
Sequence order drifts
Several beats have no time ranges
Assign non-overlapping intervals
Visual artifacts multiply
Scene complexity is too high for the first test
Shorten duration and remove secondary motion

callout.title: Change one variable at a time
callout.text: When a test fails, adjust the prompt, reference, duration or model—not all four. Controlled iteration teaches you which change helped.

examples.label: Image-to-video
examples.text: Preserve the subject, clothing, composition and background from the first frame. [subject] performs [single action]. [one camera move with endpoint]. [environmental motion]. [lighting and texture]. Avoid new objects, text and identity changes.

examples.label: Character consistency
examples.text: The same [character description] remains consistent throughout. [0–Xs] [first action and shot]. [X–Ys] [second action and camera transition]. Preserve face, hairstyle, wardrobe colors and body proportions; natural motion, no duplicate limbs.

examples.label: Product commercial
examples.text: An unbranded [product] on [surface]. [camera move] reveals [material detail]. Controlled studio lighting, accurate geometry, clean reflections, no text or extra accessories. End on a stable centered hero frame.

faqs.question: What is the best prompt structure for Seedance 2.5?
faqs.answer: Write the subject, the action, the setting, one camera move with an endpoint, the look, and the audio, in that order. Put spoken lines in double quotes and add time ranges only for shots with separate beats.

faqs.question: How long should a Seedance 2.5 prompt be?
faqs.answer: Long enough to define the shot, not to fill a target word count. A focused single shot may need one paragraph; a 15–30 second sequence benefits from timecoded beats.

faqs.question: Does Seedance 2.5 understand timecodes?
faqs.answer: Time ranges are a useful way to communicate sequential intent in supported workflows, but they are direction rather than a frame-accurate editing guarantee.

faqs.question: Should I include negative prompts?
faqs.answer: Use a short avoid list only for recurring failures: no text, no duplicate limbs, no identity change. A long negative list can compete with the main instruction.

faqs.question: What resolution should I use while testing prompts?
faqs.answer: Use 480p and 5–10 seconds for early motion tests. Move to 720p and longer duration after the structure works.
